questions.title: What is the role of the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ in the DPO objective?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the DPO paper and I see that the objective function $\mathcal{L}_{DPO}$ relies heavily on a reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. The paper says it is typically initialized as the SFT model. I'm confused as to why this is necessary. If the goal is simply to make the model $\pi_{\theta}$ prefer $y_w$ over $y_l$, why can't we just optimize the relative probabilities of the current model $\pi_{\theta}}$ without referring back to a base model?

questions.title: Is DPO fundamentally different from supervised fine-tuning on preferred completions?
questions.question_body: In the Experiments section, the authors compare DPO to 'Preferred-FT', which is just supervised learning on the chosen completion $y_w$. Looking at the DPO loss, it seems to be increasing the probability of $y_w$ and decreasing $y_l$. Is DPO just a more complex version of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) combined with unlikelihood training, or is there a theoretical reason why this specific formulation is superior to just training on the 'correct' answers?

questions.title: How does the partition function $Z(x)$ actually cancel out in the DPO derivation?
questions.question_body: The paper explains that the optimal policy is $\pi_r(y|x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y))$. They then rearrange this to express the reward as $r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)} + \beta \log Z(x)$. When substituting this into the Bradley-Terry model $p^*(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \sigma(r^*(x, y_1) - r^*(x, y_2))$, the authors state that the partition function cancels. I am struggling to follow the algebra—could someone show exactly how $Z(x)$ disappears during this step?

questions.title: Does the DPO reparameterization limit the expressiveness of the learned reward?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that all reward classes consistent with the Bradley-Terry model can be represented by the reparameterization $r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$. I'm confused by the mention of 'equivalence classes' where two rewards are equivalent if they differ by a function $f(x)$. Does this mean that DPO cannot learn a unique reward function, but only a class of functions? And if so, does this limitation affect the final quality of the policy $\pi_{\theta}$?

questions.title: Why is the $\sigma(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat{r}_\theta(x, y_w))$ term in the DPO gradient critical for stability?
questions.question_body: In the 'What does the DPO update do?' section, the authors derive the gradient and point out a weighting term $\sigma(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat{r}_\theta(x, y_w))$. They claim that a naive objective without this weighting causes the model to 'degenerate'. I don't understand the intuition here. Why does weighting the gradient by how 'wrong' the current implicit reward is prevent degeneration, and what does 'degeneration' actually look like in the context of language model outputs?
